Summary  
Data source overview: The IJCAI-18 paper “The Facets of Artificial Intelligence: A Framework to Track the Evolution of AI” introduces nine orthogonal “facets” (functionality, referent, generality, location, embodiment, paradigm, actors, character, nature) and demonstrates – through 50-year bibliometric analyses of AAAI/IJCAI proceedings and the AITopics archive – how this multi-facet view yields a stable picture of AI’s evolution. The authors argue that such a structured view is necessary for effective governance, allocation of resources, safety regulation and future-proof evaluation of AI systems.  

Extraction confidence[86] – I am highly confident all main causal-interventional pathways (risks → problem analyses → theoretical insights → design rationales → implementation mechanisms → validation evidence → interventions) were captured and inter-connected, with optimal node naming for cross-source merging and strict adherence to JSON format. Minor uncertainty comes from inferring policy-focused interventions that are only implicitly suggested in the text.  

Inference strategy justification: The paper is conceptual; explicit interventions are mostly recommendations. Moderate inference (edge confidence = 2) was used to phrase three actionable interventions an AI-safety analyst would naturally derive: adopt the facet framework in policy, deploy automated monitoring tools, and prioritise neglected subdisciplines.  

Extraction completeness: 17 nodes (~1 per 430 words) cover every distinct claim used in the authors’ reasoning and connect all paths into a single fabric. All nodes share edges; no satellites remain. Framework components were decomposed (e.g., nine-facet framework → keyword-to-facet mapping → visualisation app).  

Key limitations:  
1. No quantitative safety experiment exists in the paper; validation evidence comes from bibliometric consistency, hence edges carry medium confidence at best.  
2. Interventions are policy/process oriented (lifecycle = 6 “Other”), so downstream tooling that expects model-centric mitigations must recognise this category.  
3. Section boundaries are sometimes blurred in the source PDF; references to “closest preceding section titles” are approximate but unique.
